Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 112, verse 1–4 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His saying, exalted be His praise and sanctified be His names: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One (1). Allah, the Eternal Refuge (2). He begets not, nor is He begotten (3). And there is none comparable to Him (4).﴾

It is reported that the polytheists asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the lineage of the Lord of Might, so Allah sent down this surah as an answer to them. Some others said: Rather, it was revealed because the Jews asked him, saying: "This Allah created creation; who created Allah?" So it was sent down as an answer to them.

Mention of those who said that it was revealed in answer to the polytheists who asked him to give them the lineage of the Lord, blessed and exalted:

⁕ Ahmad ibn Mani' al-Marwazi and Mahmud ibn Khidash al-Talaqani narrated to us, and both said: Abu Sa'id al-San'ani narrated to us, he said: Abu Ja'far al-Razi narrated to us, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from Abu al-Aliyah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Give us the lineage of your Lord." So Allah revealed: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge.﴾

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, from Yazid, from Ikrimah, who said: The polytheists said: "O Messenger of Allah, inform us about your Lord, describe to us your Lord, what is He and of what is He?" So Allah revealed: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One﴾ to the end of the surah.

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾. He said: Qatadah al-Ahzab said it: "Give us the lineage of your Lord," so Jibril came to him with this.

⁕ Muhammad ibn Awf narrated to me, he said: Shurayh narrated to us, he said: Isma'il ibn Mujalid narrated to us, from Mujalid, from al-Sha'bi, from Jabir, who said: The polytheists said: "Give us the lineage of your Lord," so Allah revealed: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One.﴾

Mention of those who said that it was revealed because of the question of the Jews:

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah narrated to us, he said: Ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from Muhammad, from Sa'id, who said: A group of Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, this Allah created creation; who created Him?" The Prophet (ﷺ) became angry until his color changed, then he was overcome with anger for his Lord, so Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and calmed him, and said: "Lower your wing over yourself, O Muhammad," and there came to him from Allah the answer to what they had asked him. He said: "Allah says: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He begets not, nor is He begotten, and there is none comparable to Him.﴾" When the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it to them, they said: "Describe to us your Lord: how He created Him, how He strengthened Him, and how His forearm is." The Prophet (ﷺ) became angrier than his first anger, and was overcome with anger, so Jibril came to him and said to him the same statement, and brought him the answer to what they had asked: ﴿They have not estimated Allah with His true estimation, while the earth entire will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand. Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate.﴾

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah, from Qatadah, who said: Some people from the Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Give us the lineage of your Lord," so there was revealed: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One﴾ until the end of the surah.

So the meaning of the statement, if the matter is as we have described, is: Say, O Muhammad, to these who ask you about the lineage of your Lord, His description, and who created Him: The Lord about whom you ask me is Allah, to whom belongs the worship of everything; worship is not fitting except for Him, and it is not suitable for anything other than Him.

The scholars of Arabic grammar differed regarding what raises ﴿أَحَدٌ﴾ (aḥadun). Some of them said: what raises it is "Allah" (Allāh), and it is an ʿimād (a pronoun of separation, a dummy pronoun), in the position of the hāʾ in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾. Another of them said: Rather, it is in the nominative case even though it is indefinite, by way of a fresh start (istiʾnāf), as in your saying: "This is my husband, an old man." And he said: "Huwa Allāh" is an answer to people who said to him: "What is it that you worship?" So he said: "Huwa Allāh." Then it was said to him: "And what is He?" He said: "Huwa aḥad."

Others said: aḥad here means "wāḥid" (one). They denied that the ʿimād is used to begin a fresh sentence unless it comes after a particle of doubt such as ẓanna and its sisters, or kāna and its derivatives, or inna and what resembles it. This second opinion is more akin to the schools of Arabic grammar.

The readers differed concerning the recitation of this. The majority of the readers of the amṣār (the major cities) recited ﴿aḥadun Allāhu al-ṣamad﴾ with tanwīn on "aḥadun", except Nasr ibn ʿĀṣim and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abi Ishaq, from whom it is narrated that they omitted the tanwīn: "aḥada Allāhu". Those who recited it thus seem to have held that the nūn of inflection (tanwīn) is sometimes dropped when the alif-lām or a sākin letter follows it, as the poet said:

"How can I sleep on my bed, when a fierce raid has not yet covered al-Sham,
Which distracts the old man from his sons and uncovers the virgin guardian of the noble lady."

He means: "from the guardians of the noble lady."

Our view on this is: tanwīn, for two reasons. The first is that it is the more eloquent of the two forms, the more well-known of the two usages, and the better among the Arabs. The second is the consensus of the authoritative readers of the amṣār on choosing tanwīn in it, and with that, there is no need to support its correctness with other evidence. We have already explained the meaning of His saying "aḥad" earlier, in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary.

* *

His saying: ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge (al-ṣamad)﴾

He, exalted be His remembrance, says: The worshipped one, to whom alone worship is fitting, is al-Ṣamad.

The scholars of interpretation differed about the meaning of al-ṣamad. Some of them said: It is the one who is not hollow, and does not eat or drink.

Mention of those who said that:

⁕ ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn al-Aswad narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Rabi'ah narrated to us, from Salamah ibn Sabur, from ʿAtiyyah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the one who is not hollow.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, he said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the solid (al-muṣmat) which has no hollow.

⁕ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Mujahid, the same, exactly.

⁕ al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the solid that has no hollow.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: ʿAbd al-Rahman and Waki' narrated to us, both said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the one who has no hollow.

⁕ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us; and Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, all together, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, he said: al-Rabi' ibn Muslim narrated to us, from al-Hasan, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the one who has no hollow.

⁕ He said: al-Rabi' ibn Muslim narrated to us, from Ibrahim ibn Maysarah, who said: Mujahid sent me to Sa'id ibn Jubayr to ask him about "al-Ṣamad," and he said: The one who has no hollow.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: Yahya narrated to us, he said: Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid narrated to us, from al-Sha'bi, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the one who does not feed on food.

⁕ Ya'qub narrated to us, he said: Hushaym narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from al-Sha'bi, that he said: "al-Ṣamad": the one who does not eat food nor drink drink.

⁕ Abu Kurayb and Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, both said: Waki' narrated to us, from Salamah ibn Nubayt, from al-Dahhak, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the one who has no hollow.

⁕ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Ibn Abi Za'idah narrated to us, from Isma'il, from ʿAmir, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the one who does not eat food.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar and Zayd ibn Akhzam narrated to us, both said: Ibn Dawud narrated to us, from al-Mustaqim ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the one who has no inner filling (hishwah).

⁕ I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: ʿUbayd narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say concerning His saying: "al-Ṣamad": the one who has no hollow.

⁕ al-ʿAbbas ibn Abi Talib narrated to me, he said: Muhammad ibn ʿUmar ibn Rumi narrated to us, from ʿUbayd Allah ibn Sa'id, the leader of al-A'mash, who said: Salih ibn Hayyan narrated to me, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Buraydah, from his father, who said: I do not know it except that he raised it (to the Prophet ﷺ), he said: "al-Ṣamad": the one who has no hollow.

⁕ Ibn ʿAbd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Bishr ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, from al-Rabi' ibn Muslim, who said: I heard al-Hasan say: "al-Ṣamad": the one who has no hollow.

⁕ Ibn ʿAbd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from ʿIkrimah, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the one who has no hollow.

Others said: It is the one from whom nothing comes out.

Mention of those who said that:

⁕ Ya'qub narrated to me, he said: Ibn ʿUlayyah narrated to us, from Abu Raja', who said: I heard ʿIkrimah say concerning His saying: "al-Ṣamad": the one from whom nothing has come out, and who did not beget and was not begotten.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, he said: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Abu Raja' Muhammad ibn Yusuf, from ʿIkrimah, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the one from whom nothing comes out.

Others said: It is the one who neither begets nor is begotten.

Mention of those who said that:

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the one who neither begets nor is begotten, because everything that begets will be inherited from, and everything that is begotten will die; so He, exalted be His remembrance, informed them that He is not inherited from and does not die.

⁕ Ahmad ibn Mani' and Mahmud ibn Khidash narrated to us, both said: Abu Sa'id al-San'ani narrated to us, he said: The polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Give us the lineage of your Lord," so Allah revealed: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He begets not, nor is He begotten, and there is none comparable to Him.﴾ Because everything that is begotten will die, and everything that dies will be inherited from, and Allah, may His praise be exalted, neither dies nor is inherited from. ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾: there is no likeness or equal to Him, and nothing is like His likeness.

⁕ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from Abu Ma'shar, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b: "al-Ṣamad": the one who neither begets nor is begotten, and there is none comparable to Him.

Others said: He has reached the peak of His lordship (su'dud).

Mention of those who said that:

⁕ Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to me, he said: Abu Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from al-A'mash, from Shaqiq, who said: "al-Ṣamad": He is the master (al-sayyid) who has reached the peak of His lordship.

⁕ Abu Kurayb, Ibn Bashshar and Ibn ʿAbd al-A'la narrated to us, they said: Waki' narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Wa'il, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the master who has reached the peak of his lordship; Abu Kurayb and Ibn ʿAbd al-A'la did not say "his lordship."

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Abu Wa'il, the same.

⁕ ʿAli narrated to us, he said: Abu Salih narrated to us, he said: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: "al-Ṣamad": he says: the master who has been perfected in his mastery, the noble one who has been perfected in his nobility, the great one who has been magnified in his greatness, the forbearing one who has been perfected in his forbearance, the rich one who has been perfected in his riches, the mighty one who has been perfected in his might, the knowing one who has been perfected in his knowledge, the wise one who has been perfected in his wisdom; He is the one who has been perfected in all kinds of nobility and mastery, and He is Allah, glorified be He; this is His description, and it is fitting for none but Him.

Others said: Rather, He is the Everlasting who does not perish.

Mention of those who said that:

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: "Say, He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He begets not, nor is He begotten," he said: al-Hasan and Qatadah used to say: "The one who remains after His creation." He said: This is a pure surah, in which there is no mention of anything of the affairs of this world or the Hereafter.

⁕ Ibn ʿAbd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, who said: "al-Ṣamad": the Everlasting.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: al-Ṣamad, in the language of the Arabs, is the master to whom one turns for refuge (al-sayyid alladhi yuṣmad ilayh), the one above whom there is no one; and thus they call their nobles. And from it is the poet's saying:

"Ah, the announcer of the death of the two best of the Banu Asad has come,
Of ʿAmr ibn Mas'ud and of the master al-Samad."

And al-Zibriqan said:
"Nor a hostage, except a master, al-Samad."

If this is so, then the meaning most fitting for the interpretation of the word is the familiar meaning in the speech of those in whose tongue the Qur'an was revealed. And if the report of Ibn Buraydah from his father were sound, it would be the most correct of the sayings, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knows best what Allah, exalted be His praise, meant and what He revealed to him.

* *

His saying: ﴿He begets not﴾

He says: He is not perishing, because everything that begets is perishing and passing away.

﴿Nor is He begotten﴾: He says: and He is not a newly originated thing that did not exist and then came into being, because every begotten thing came into existence after it was not, and originated after it was not existent; rather, He, exalted be His remembrance, is eternal and has never ceased, everlasting and has not vanished, and does not pass away or perish.

* *

His saying: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾

The scholars of interpretation differed about the meaning of this. Some of them said: its meaning is: there is no likeness or equal to Him.

Mention of those who said that:

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah, concerning His saying: "And there is none comparable to Him": there is no likeness to Him, nor equal, and nothing is like His likeness.

⁕ Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, from ʿAmr ibn Ghaylan al-Thaqafi, who was the governor of Basra, from Ka'b, who said: Allah, exalted be His remembrance, founded the seven heavens and the seven earths upon this surah: ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten, and there is none comparable to Him﴾, and that no one of His creation is equal to Him.

⁕ ʿAli narrated to me, he said: Abu Salih narrated to us, he said: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾: He said: there is nothing like His likeness; so glory be to Allah, the One, the Subduer.

⁕ al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾: "like" (mithl).

Others said: its meaning is that He had no consort.

Mention of those who said that:

⁕ Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: ʿAbd al-Rahman narrated to us, he said: Sufyan narrated to us, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abjar, from Talhah, from Mujahid, concerning His saying: "And there is none comparable to Him": he said: a consort.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: Yahya narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abjar, from Talhah, from Mujahid, the same.

⁕ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Ibn Idris narrated to us, from ʿAbd al-Malik, from Talhah, from Mujahid, the same.

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abjar, from a man, from Mujahid, concerning ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾: he said: a consort.

⁕ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Waki' narrated to us, from Sufyan, from ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Abjar, from Talhah ibn Musarrif, from Mujahid, concerning ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾: he said: a consort.

⁕ Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to us, he said: Ibn Idris narrated to us, from ʿAbd al-Malik, from Talhah, from Mujahid, the same.

Al-kufu', al-kufa, and al-kifa' in the speech of the Arabs are one and the same, and they mean the equal and the like; and from it is the saying of the Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan:

"Do not hurl me with a pillar that has no equal (kifa')
Even if the enemies were to encircle you with the calamities (al-rifd)."

He means: "lā kifāʾ lahu," there is no equal to it.

The readers differed concerning the recitation of His saying ﴿kufuwan﴾. The majority of the readers of Basra recited it ﴿kufuwan﴾ with a damma on the kaf and the fa'. And some readers of Kufa recited it with the fa' sukun and hamzah: "kufan̆".

The correct position on this matter is that it should be said: both are well-known recitations and widely attested dialects, so whichever of the two a reciter reads, he is correct.

End of the tafsir of Surat al-Ikhlas.

His saying: ﴿He begets not﴾

He says: He is not perishing, because everything that begets is perishing and passing away.

﴿Nor is He begotten﴾: He says: and He is not a newly originated thing that did not exist and then came into being, because every begotten thing came into existence after it was not, and originated after it was not existent; rather, He, exalted be His remembrance, is eternal and has never ceased, everlasting and has not vanished, and does not pass away or perish.

* *

His saying: ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾

Al-kufu', al-kufa, and al-kifa' in the speech of the Arabs are one and the same, and they mean the equal and the like; and from it is the saying of the Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan:

"Do not hurl me with a pillar that has no equal (kifa')
Even if the enemies were to encircle you with the calamities (al-rifd)."

He means: "lā kifāʾ lahu," there is no equal to it.

The readers differed concerning the recitation of His saying ﴿kufuwan﴾. The majority of the readers of Basra recited it ﴿kufuwan﴾ with a damma on the kaf and the fa'. And some readers of Kufa recited it with the fa' sukun and hamzah: "kufan̆".

The correct position on this matter is that it should be said: both are well-known recitations and widely attested dialects, so whichever of the two a reciter reads, he is correct.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 112, verse 1–4 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His saying, exalted be His praise and sanctified be His names: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One (1). Allah, the Eternal Refuge (2). He begets not, nor is He begotten (3). And there is none comparable to Him (4).﴾

It is reported that the polytheists asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the lineage of the Lord of Might, so Allah sent down this surah as an answer to them. Some others said: Rather, it was revealed because the Jews asked him, saying: "This Allah created creation; who created Allah?" So it was sent down as an answer to them.

So Allah revealed: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge.﴾

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, from Yazid, from Ikrimah, who said: The polytheists said: "O Messenger of Allah, inform us about your Lord, describe to us your Lord, what is He and of what is He?" So Allah revealed: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One﴾ to the end of the surah.

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Abu Ja'far, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾. He said: Qatadah al-Ahzab said it: "Give us the lineage of your Lord," so Jibril came to him with this.

⁕ Muhammad ibn Awf narrated to me, he said: Shurayh narrated to us, he said: Isma'il ibn Mujalid narrated to us, from Mujalid, from al-Sha'bi, from Jabir, who said: The polytheists said: "Give us the lineage of your Lord," so Allah revealed: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One.﴾

Mention of those who said that it was revealed because of the question of the Jews:

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Salamah narrated to us, he said: Ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from Muhammad, from Sa'id, who said: A group of Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, this Allah created creation; who created Him?" The Prophet (ﷺ) became angry until his color changed, then he was overcome with anger for his Lord, so Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and calmed him, and said: "Lower your wing over yourself, O Muhammad," and there came to him from Allah the answer to what they had asked him. He said: "Allah says: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge. He begets not, nor is He begotten, and there is none comparable to Him.﴾" When the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it to them, they said: "Describe to us your Lord: how He created Him, how He strengthened Him, and how His forearm is." The Prophet (ﷺ) became angrier than his first anger, and was overcome with anger, so Jibril came to him and said to him the same statement, and brought him the answer to what they had asked: ﴿They have not estimated Allah with His true estimation, while the earth entire will be His handful on the Day of Resurrection, and the heavens will be folded up in His right hand. Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate.﴾

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Mihran narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Abi Arubah, from Qatadah, who said: Some people from the Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Give us the lineage of your Lord," so there was revealed: ﴿Say, He is Allah, the One﴾ until the end of the surah.

So the meaning of the statement, if the matter is as we have described, is: Say, O Muhammad, to these who ask you about the lineage of your Lord, His description, and who created Him: The Lord about whom you ask me is Allah, to whom belongs the worship of everything; worship is not fitting except for Him, and it is not suitable for anything other than Him.

The scholars of Arabic grammar differed regarding what raises ﴿أَحَدٌ﴾ (aḥadun). Some of them said: what raises it is "Allah" (Allāh), and it is an ʿimād (a pronoun of separation, a dummy pronoun), in the position of the hāʾ in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾. Another of them said: Rather, it is in the nominative case even though it is indefinite, by way of a fresh start (istiʾnāf), as in your saying: "This is my husband, an old man." And he said: "Huwa Allāh" is an answer to people who said to him: "What is it that you worship?" So he said: "Huwa Allāh." Then it was said to him: "And what is He?" He said: "Huwa aḥad."

Others said: aḥad here means "wāḥid" (one). They denied that the ʿimād is used to begin a fresh sentence unless it comes after a particle of doubt such as ẓanna and its sisters, or kāna and its derivatives, or inna and what resembles it. This second opinion is more akin to the schools of Arabic grammar.

The readers differed concerning the recitation of this. The majority of the readers of the amṣār (the major cities) recited ﴿aḥadun Allāhu al-ṣamad﴾ with tanwīn on "aḥadun", except Nasr ibn ʿĀṣim and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abi Ishaq, from whom it is narrated that they omitted the tanwīn: "aḥada Allāhu". Those who recited it thus seem to have held that the nūn of inflection (tanwīn) is sometimes dropped when the alif-lām or a sākin letter follows it, as the poet said:

"How can I sleep on my bed, when a fierce raid has not yet covered al-Sham,
Which distracts the old man from his sons and uncovers the virgin guardian of the noble lady."

He means: "from the guardians of the noble lady."

Our view on this is: tanwīn, for two reasons. The first is that it is the more eloquent of the two forms, the more well-known of the two usages, and the better among the Arabs. The second is the consensus of the authoritative readers of the amṣār on choosing tanwīn in it, and with that, there is no need to support its correctness with other evidence. We have already explained the meaning of His saying "aḥad" earlier, in a way that makes repeating it here unnecessary.

Some others said: Rather, it was revealed because the Jews asked him, saying: "This Allah created creation; who created Allah?" So it was sent down as an answer to them.

⁕ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, from Yazid, from Ikrimah, who said: The polytheists said: "O Messenger of Allah, inform us about your Lord, describe to us your Lord, what is He and of what is He?" Some of them said: what raises it is "Allah" (Allāh), and it is an ʿimād (a pronoun of separation, a dummy pronoun), in the position of the hāʾ in His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾.
